doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: Writing vertically like Mancini versus horizontally like Ellington
summary: Weber and Rowe discuss Mancini's vertical writing, Ellington's horizontal lines, and writing for known players.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You know there’s nothing like that feeling, pre-Finale or Sibelius, of writing a piece, and you know you check it at the piano, but you’re never really sure it’s going to work until all those human beings get there and they read it.

You’re right, and there are people who write vertically and there are people who write horizontally. I mean Mancini for example writes vertically, meaning you could take any cross section of any conductor’s score and it’s going to be a fabulous chord. He thinks that way, he thinks vertically. And Duke Ellington for example, thought horizontally. Everybody’s line had to be something really hip. And it somehow works horizontally. And I don’t know if anybody ever analyzed it that way. Maybe this is the advantage of not studying music, it’s just that’s the way it sounds to me.

I think that’s a great point. Because I remember listening to him some recently and I was trying to figure out what is it that make him sound like he does. And that’s a very good sort of observation. And what you just said too. What did you just say?
Yeah but then after that you said not knowing music theory or — that there’s some advantage to that.

Yeah. In other words, by ear I manage to pick out what each individual line was in the Duke score from 1927 and I said oh every single line works somehow. You know vertically it may not work quite as well, but horizontally everybody’s got something cool to play. So it keeps them happy in that way. And Mancini and a number of other composers have the technique of writing vertically, which means it’s pleasing for the conductor and perhaps for a larger audience. I don’t know. I should analyze it further.
I wonder if that has to do anything with, you know Duke knew who he was writing for.

Yes. And similarly, Henry Mancini even says in his book, he says, “If you have the luxury of knowing who your players are, there’s no greater advantage to an arranger and conductor than that. Because if you have a swell tuba player who can really get around the tuba, write in some tuba parts. Write some cool stuff for them to do. So I guess both answers are right.
